Name: Shrine of Shah Jamal
Description:
The shrine of Baba Shah Jamal, in the locality that now bears his name adjoining Ichhra and opposite Forman Christian College, commemorates Syed Shah Jamal, a Sufi of Hussaini Syed descent who traced his lineage to Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari of Uch Sharif. The 2026 field survey names his father as Syed Ahmad Shah — the name this archive's entry for his brother, Baba Shah Kamal, gives independently — and adds that the family moved from Kashmir to Sialkot and from Sialkot to Lahore, where both brothers were born and where both are counted among the saints. It also accounts for his coming to Ichhra: he arrived to see Shah Kamal, whose shrine still stands close to his own, and pitched his camp a short distance from his brother's house. He belonged jointly to the Qadiriyya, Suhrawardiyya and Chishtiyya orders — a special disciple, tradition holds, of Sheikh Khokar Baig Suhrawardi — and lived in Lahore during the reign of the Mughal emperor Akbar, whose syncretic Din-i-Ilahi he is remembered for having resisted, working instead to draw people back towards orthodox Islamic practice. Devotees, the survey records, know him for his open-handedness as *Sakhi Sarwar* — a title that in the Punjab more usually belongs to Sultan Sakhi Sarwar of Dera Ghazi Khan, whose shrine this archive also holds; it is set down here as the survey gave it, and not as an identification of the two. Born, by the shrine's account, in 1587, he is generally held to have died in the later seventeenth century, though sources differ on the precise year: 1649 and 1671 both appear, the shrine's own tradition holding to 1671 and commemorating his death on the 4th of Rabi-ul-Sani. A separate compendium of Pakistani Sufi saints, Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan*, independently places his shrine on Achhra Road facing west, in Shah Jamal Colony, Lahore — consistent with this entry's own location — and traces his Suhrawardi lineage specifically to Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan.

The site itself, tradition says, was built and named "Damdama" by Shah Jamal in his own lifetime, and it was one of several stations of his austerities: besides his Damdama cell he kept chillas (forty-day retreats) at Sheikhupura, Shah Rehman, Shahdara Lahore and Chanpatpur in India. His death is remembered as inseparable from his devotions: emerging from a chilla, he died as the roof of his cell collapsed, and as people laboured to free him a voice from within is said to have commanded that he not be pulled out, but that his grave be raised over that very spot — which was done.

Legends gather thickly around the Damdama. The best known tells of a princess — Akbar's sister — who, annoyed that the tall tower overlooked her palace, demanded he lower it; the saint performed dhamal on its top floor, and storey after storey sank into the earth until only two remained, whereupon he predicted that her palace would not outlast his — fulfilled, it is said, when Sikh forces later destroyed it. Another tells of a cheating Hindu businessman to whom the saint gave a cantaloupe to feed his wife; twin sons followed, one of whom, named Sheikh Fakhr-ud-Din by Shah Jamal himself, became a devoted lifelong disciple — and the saint is also said to have saved that family by calling them outside moments before their roof collapsed. The survey adds that Sheikh Fakhr-ud-Din stayed in the saint's service all his life and that his grave lies inside the shrine.

Today the shrine is best known not for quiet contemplation but for its exuberant Thursday-night dhamal, when devotees, students, musicians and curious visitors gather from dusk until the early hours as dhol drummers — most famously the late Pappu Sain, whose successors continue the tradition — drive crowds into rhythmic, trance-like dancing, alongside qawwali, langar and the lighting of lamps. This weekly spectacle has made Shah Jamal one of the most written-about expressions of popular Sufi devotional culture in Punjab, and the crowds are considerable: on the order of 10,000 to 15,000 visitors a day, rising to 200,000-250,000 for the annual urs, held on the 3rd to the 5th of Rabi-ul-Sani with the ritual washing (gusal) of the tomb, the offering of the chadar, and drumming and dhamal.

The tomb itself is enclosed within a mosque of relatively modern construction, single-domed with four minarets, reflecting rebuilding rather than preserved Mughal fabric; an adjoining graveyard lies beside it. The shrine — of the Suhrawardi line and the Ahl-e-Sunnat tradition — has been in the care of the government's Auqaf Department since 1960; before that, the survey relates, its upkeep and adornment fell first to Shah Jamal himself, who oversaw the building in his own lifetime, and afterwards to the kings, maharajas and devotees who came after him. The current sajjada nashin, a descendant of the saint, continues to hold Khatam Khawajgan ceremonies. The site illustrates the continuing vitality of shrine-centred devotional practice in Lahore, and its shadows as well: the city's homeless rely on the shrine's langar and offerings, even as questions over noise, crowding and drug use in the vicinity — a real safety concern for pilgrims — have periodically drawn official scrutiny.

Name: Shrine of Peer Makki
Description:
Standing close to the great mausoleum of Data Ganj Bakhsh, in the Walled City's Bhati Gate quarter, the shrine of Peer Makki commemorates Hazrat Syed Azizuddin al-Hassani wal-Hussaini, a scholar-mystic born in Baghdad — the son of Hazrat Peer Syed Abdullah, of a Hasani-Hussaini family of religious scholars that counted Junaid Baghdadi, Imam Ahmad bin Hanbal and Sheikh Abdul Qadir Jilani among its kin. He is said to have migrated to Mecca in 562 AH, at about the age of thirty, and to have spent twelve years there in ascetic seclusion — hence his popular title "Makki" — before journeying overland to India. Hagiographical accounts hold that he arrived in Lahore in 575 AH (around 1178 CE) by what tradition describes as divine instruction, and remained for some thirty-six years as a teacher of both the exoteric sciences of Islamic law and the esoteric path of the Junaidi Sufi lineage, tracing back to the classical Baghdad master Junayd. He is said to have died in 612 AH (1215 CE). Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan* preserves the same broad outline — his given name Azizuddin, his Baghdad origin, and the twelve years spent in seclusion at Mecca that earned him the epithet "Makki" — and adds that on first reaching Lahore he went directly to the shrine of Data Ganj Bakhsh before settling at the site that became his own; the detail reinforces, without resolving, the chronological tension already noted below between the two saints' conventional dates.

A well-loved anecdote recalls that during Sultan Muhammad Ghori's 1178 siege of Lahore, the besieged governor Khusro Malik sought Peer Makki's prayers, and the saint assured him of six further years of safety. Devotional custom in Lahore holds that pilgrims should pay their respects at Peer Makki's tomb before proceeding to Data Darbar, honouring him as a spiritual forerunner in the same sacred locale — although the popular claim that he personally tutored Data Ganj Bakhsh sits awkwardly with the conventional dating of Ali Hujwiri's death around 1072, a century before Peer Makki's own arrival, and should be understood as devotional tradition rather than strict chronology. A tradition recorded at the shrine itself runs the other way about: when Ali Hujwiri was ordered to migrate to Lahore, he is said to have objected that "Peer Makki is present there, who is enough for Lahore" — only to arrive and find Peer Makki's funeral already underway. Like the tutoring claim, the story fits loosely with the dates, but it carries the shrine's essential teaching: that Lahore has never been without a saint of Allah.

The shrine complex includes an adjoining mosque, the Hazrat Pir Makki Masjid, and is formally administered, like Data Darbar itself, by the Punjab Auqaf and Religious Affairs Department, which the field survey says took charge of the shrine in 1958; its tradition is Syed and Ahl-e-Sunnat. Despite its proximity to one of Pakistan's most visited shrines, Peer Makki's own tomb receives markedly fewer pilgrims — some 3,500 to 4,000 on an ordinary day — giving it a more intimate, contemplative atmosphere, though Thursday-night gatherings draw larger crowds, and the narrow street and surrounding Peer Makki Bazaar can make access difficult. The annual urs, held on the 9th to the 11th of Rabi-ul-Awal, fills the quarter with gatherings and dhikr, drums and dhamal, qawwali, the ritual bathing of the shrine and the distribution of offerings, and draws on the order of 400,000 to 500,000 devotees. Many writers — including, it is said at the shrine, authors from the Hindu and Christian communities — have written books about the saint that are still read with interest today.

## The Life, as the Survey Narrates It

The 2026 field survey gives a fuller life than this entry has carried, and it is set out here in the account's own terms.

His father, Hazrat Peer Syed Abdullah, was himself a saint and a scholar who taught in Baghdad, and Peer Makki had his first education from him — memorising the Qur'an, then learning what the survey calls the knowledge of the soul and of the sect, seated in the same row as everyone else in his father's circle. Having taken the outward sciences as far as they went, he judged that he must go looking for the hidden knowledge, and in 562 AH, at thirty, he left Baghdad for Mecca. He spent twelve years there, hearing the pleas of those who came to him, helping them, keeping his nights in the Haram in the remembrance of God, and — the account says — receiving the blessing of the Prophet many times. He began to know what was to come, and did not show it.

The migration to India, in this telling, was not his own idea. Worshipping in the Haram, he received the Prophet's command to go to Hind, where the people had fallen into associating partners with God, and to bring them back to the Sunna and to the oneness of God. He did not wish to leave the House of God, but the command was the command: he made his last Hajj, took some companions with him, and turned first to Baghdad, to tell his family and to say the Fatiha at his father's grave, before setting out. Two roads led to India, one through the dry desert and one by sea; the journey was long and dangerous and there was little to eat or drink, but he preached along the way, and people were moved enough to join his caravan. Something close to a year later he reached India and gave thanks. He came to Lahore in 575 AH and settled in the mosque that today carries his name beside his shrine, leading the prayers, teaching the Qur'an, and calling people away from polytheism.

The survey then narrates the political part of his life at length. Lahore was held by Khusrau Malik — whom the account calls the last of Mahmud of Ghazni's line, and the son of King Khusrau — and describes as pleasure-seeking and unjust; Muhammad Shahab-ud-Din Ghori was advancing on the city, having already taken Multan and Sialkot. When Khusrau Malik came to ask how long his rule would last, the saint told him plainly that it would end soon, that what God has written must come, and that he should turn to God and deal justly with his people. When Ghori's army arrived, the people and the king both ran to him; he told them to be patient and to repent, and said the danger would pass and return in six years. Ghori withdrew, and the saint's name went round the city — but the people soon returned to their old habits, and exactly six years later Ghori came again. Again the saint promised a respite, and said it was the last; again the army turned back, and this time people called him a liar, saying the old man only ever said such things and that Ghori left out of fear. When Ghori finally took Lahore, Khusrau Malik's men were killed or went over to him, and the king himself was taken prisoner and later killed. Ghori, the account says, came to the saint's door and told him he had known he was there, and that everything he had said had been true.

He preached in Lahore for thirty-six years after that, and died in 612 AH; the quarter took his name from him, as the title Makki had come from his years in Mecca. Kings maintained the shrine after him and added to its beauty, and the survey states that the Auqaf Department took responsibility for it in 1958.

Name: Shrine of Mauj Darya Bukhari
Description:
Tucked away on Edward Road near the old Customs House in Anarkali, the octagonal tomb of Hazrat Meeran Muhammad Shah Bukhari — popularly called "Mauj Darya," or "Wave of the River" — commemorates a saint born in 1533 in Uch Sharif, the son of Safi-ud-Din Bukhari of the Sadaat of that town, a descendant of Jalaluddin Surkh-Posh Bukhari whose genealogy is traced through Syed Jalal-ud-Din Jahaniyan Jahangasht, and an adherent of the Suhrawardi silsila founded by Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan. He became a hafiz-e-Quran in his youth and, according to popular tradition, earned his epithet by miraculously diverting the flood-prone River Ravi away from Lahore. The 2026 field survey derives the same title differently: he was called Mouj Darya, it says, for his open-handed generosity and for the state of spiritual ecstasy (*mouj*) in which his prayers were held to be answered at once. Both derivations stand here as they were given. He is remembered, too, as a missionary presence who drew many Hindus and Sikhs to Islam.

Above all he is remembered as a spiritual confidant of the Mughal emperor Akbar. The shrine's tradition relates that the emperor was foretold — through the saint's father — of a windstorm and a lit lamp that would mark the saint's presence at the fort of Chittor; when both signs appeared and the Rajput army surrendered, Akbar became his disciple. Alam Faqri's *Tazkirah Awliya-e-Pakistan* preserves an independent, extended telling of this same episode — giving the saint's given name as Miran Muhammad Shah, tracing his descent from Makhdoom Jahaniyan Jahangasht and his origins in Uch Sharif, and recounting at length how his prayer and intercession were credited with securing the fort's surrender to Akbar — corroborating, from a separate hagiographical compendium, the tradition already recorded at the shrine. Legend credits him with distributing to the poor a substantial reward Akbar granted him near Batala, and it is said that on the saint's arrival in Lahore the emperor gifted the land on which he settled; his darasgah — the seat of learning where he now lies buried — is said still to hold land documents bearing Akbar's own signature. He died in 1604, the date traditionally taken as the founding of the shrine.

He married twice. His first wife, Syedna Bibi Fatima Sani — remembered as "Bibi Killah," and popularly as Mai Fatima — bore him two sons and rests in a separate shrine facing his own, near the historic Jain Mandir; a second wife bore a third son, of whom tradition tells that he could take the form of a lion. The saint lies in a small graveyard in the company of his family, his spiritual successors and gaddi nasheen, and his cook, Allahu Samad — himself the subject of one of the shrine's most striking tales, in which the saint, to answer sceptics, had his cook sit unharmed in a burning cauldron. Other wonders are recounted of him: a cauldron of rice he blessed during a shortage that fed the people for nearly seven days; brackish irrigation water over which he prayed for local landowners, which turned sweet; and a tree planted in his lifetime — "the blessed tree" — said never to have needed cutting. His langar, devotees say, has continued under his descendants to this day. The survey adds that books about him written by Muslim, Hindu and Sikh authors alike are widely read.

Architecturally the tomb is unusual among Lahore's shrines for its octagonal plan, with a low dome, corner towers at each of its eight angles, and a mixture of recessed blind arches and plain panelled facades — a style thought to echo Multani funerary tradition. The shrine gained unwelcome national attention in 2018 when construction of the Orange Line Metro Train's underground Anarkali station demolished its mosque, langar khana and courtyard, with tunnelling reported to pass close to the saint's grave in apparent violation of heritage buffer-zone regulations — an episode that became a flashpoint in Lahore's debates over balancing infrastructure development against protection of religious heritage. Yet devotees hold that for all the government construction pressing around it, nothing has ever tarnished the shrine's beauty.

The shrine remains one of scores of Lahore shrines administered by the Punjab Auqaf and Religious Affairs Department (Mehkama Auqaf), and continues to draw a devoted following. Its upkeep, the survey relates, ran down a long line before that — from the emperor Akbar through the rulers who followed him and Maharaja Ranjit Singh, and through the saint's own descendants — before the department took it on. Daily devotion includes the recitation of the Fatiha, the lighting of diyas, the making of vows (mannat) and the presentation of niyaz, and the gatherings of Thursday night (Jummay Raat) remain the busiest of the week. The annual urs is held on the 17th to the 19th of Rabi-ul-Awal, with a Mela Chiraagha (festival of lights), the ceremonial washing (gusal) of the tomb and the changing of its chadar, and langar throughout; some 2,200 to 2,500 visitors are recorded on an ordinary day, rising to between 225,000 and 300,000 across the urs.
